definition: The State of California has several laws regulating artificial intelligence, including the Artificial Intelligence Training Data Transparency Act (AB 2013) and the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (TFAIA) (SB 53), which went into effect on January 1, 2026.
details: In addition, the California AI Transparency Act will go into effect in August 2026. By signing TFAIA into law on September 29, 2025, California became the first state to enact a statute specifically addressing the development of frontier AI models. The TFAIA protects whistleblowers who have reasonable cause to believe their employers are endangering lives or causing damages worth $1 billion. It also requires companies to publish their safety test results. On September 10, 2026, Governor Gavin Newsom signed a new series of laws to enhance protections for children from AI chatbots and technology. It requires tech companies to conduct risk assessments before new chatbot rollouts and penalizes companies if they're found guilty of harming children, with a fine of up to $1 million per child. Failed AI regulation bills in California have included SB 1047, the Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act, which was vetoed by Governor Gavin Newsom in September 2024.

explainer.lead: California AI laws are a group of state rules rather than one single AI law. They address training-data transparency, safety at frontier AI companies, and protections for children using chatbots, with different requirements and start dates.

tiers.eli5: Think of these laws as different safety rules for different parts of AI, like having separate rules for cars, bicycles, and playgrounds. Some require companies to share safety information, while others require checks before new chatbots are released to help protect children.
tiers.practitioner: Engineering and compliance teams need to match each system to the relevant law and effective date. TFAIA requires publication of safety test results, while the 2026 chatbot laws require risk assessments before new rollouts; SB 1047 was vetoed and should not be treated as an enacted requirement.
tiers.paperLevel: California AI laws = {AB 2013, SB 53 (TFAIA), California AI Transparency Act, 2026 child-protection laws for AI chatbots}, with distinct scopes and commencement dates. AB 2013 and TFAIA took effect on January 1, 2026, while the California AI Transparency Act takes effect in August 2026. This is not a single unified statutory framework, and SB 1047 is excluded because it was vetoed in September 2024.

explainer.example: A company developing a frontier AI model in California must publish its safety test results under TFAIA. An employee with reasonable cause to believe the company is endangering lives or causing $1 billion in damages is covered by its whistleblower protection.

explainer.intuition: The idea is to regulate specific AI risks through separate laws instead of applying one identical rule to every system. Transparency, frontier-model safety, and child protection each receive their own requirements.
howItWorks: AB 2013 and TFAIA, also called SB 53, took effect on January 1, 2026.
TFAIA requires companies to publish safety test results and provides whistleblower protections.
The California AI Transparency Act takes effect in August 2026.
Chatbot laws signed on September 10, 2026 require risk assessments before new rollouts and provide penalties for harming children.
explainer.whyItMatters: These laws create concrete transparency and safety duties for AI companies and protections for workers and children. When Governor Gavin Newsom signed TFAIA on September 29, 2025, California became the first state to enact a statute specifically addressing frontier AI model development.
misconceptions: California has one comprehensive AI law: these are separate measures with different scopes and dates.
SB 1047 is current law: Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed it in September 2024.
Every provision began at once: the laws have different effective dates.
